speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of

Resources and Development. Has the government of Saskatchewan requested the federal government to enter into an agreement for housing in Estevan under section 35 of the National Housing Act? If so, is the federal government prepared to enter into an agreement for this purpose?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO AGREEMENT FOR PROJECT IN ESTEVAN, SASK.
speechtext:
Section 35 of the National Housing Act has to do with dominion-provincial projects. Having in mind the difficulties attendant upon house building at this time, and the great interest of my hon. friend in housing in Estevan, a matter which he has kept before me since he entered the house, I think perhaps I should answer his question in a little more detail than I might otherwise do.
In a letter dated June 5, 1951, the minister of social welfare and rehabilitation asked for our approval of housing in a number of municipalities, including Estevan. No specific project was submitted. In my discussion with Mr. Sturdy and in my correspondence with him I pointed out the difficulties involved in building houses at this time, and stated that we must see to it that of the houses built in Canada, as many as possible are located in defence production areas. We discussed the high costs of housing, the desirability of contemplating economic rentals, and the need to build houses only in projects sufficiently large to enable us to realize all possible construction and operating economies. It was considered that projects under section 35 should not be smaller than forty or fifty units. That is why in our discussion we talked in terms of applying section 35 only in the larger municipalities.
We have not yet received details from the government of Saskatchewan about costs and consequent rental levels, and are therefore unable to form an opinion as to whether or not housing can be produced in small projects in the smaller municipalities which will be within the range of the local rental scale. However, with due regard to the above factors, we doubt that it is practical for any of the levels of government concerned to contemplate at this time housing under this section for municipalities having populations as small as Estevan.
I would suggest to my hon. friend that there are other sections which might more appropriately be considered if operations within the scope of the National Housing Act are contemplated for Estevan.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I desire to make a few remarks with respect to the

Supply-External Affairs estimates of the Department of External Affairs. As you know, they have just been returned to committee of supply after consideration by the standing committee on external affairs. I want to deal with only one or two matters which perhaps should be enlarged upon and emphasized at this time.
My first reference will be to the question of the proposed Japanese peace treaty and rearmament plan. I have no desire to discuss the Japanese peace treaty at this time, except to suggest to the minister that, when he is replying to the various questions that will be raised in committee of supply, he should deal with the matter of Canada's position in that regard. There must be a good deal of confusion in the public mind as to what is going on with respect to the negotiations leading up to the proposed agreement. First pf all we have Mr. Dulles going to Japan and then to Great Britain. Press reports from time to time have indicated that agreements have been reached. There is one this morning from London indicating that, on the question of representation of Red China as opposed to nationalist China, some agreement has been arrived at between the United States and Great Britain, a very familiar kind of agreement in diplomatic circles-that no decision will be made with respect to that matter until later.
I think a problem must be arising in people's minds as to where Canada fits into these unilateral or bilateral negotiations which are being carried on by the United States of America and their representatives. We have not had a call from Mr. Dulles in Ottawa. We would like to know whether or not we have been kept in touch with all the developments, whether or not in his various travels abroad he has carried with him some implied or express authority from Canada with respect to our stand, and what the reaction of this country may be expected to be after the agreements have been finally drafted and put into a form satisfactory to these other countries. We have a say with respect to the Japanese treaty, and I think the minister should advise the committee what method we have employed to make our voice heard in these negotiations.
I also want to raise another question, and it is also one that I think is in the minds of the public. While the military and political aspects of the Japanese negotiations are of immense importance, and I think no one would desire to minimize their importance in any way, there is a problem concerning economics, finance and trade which I trust the government will not allow to be disregarded when the final negotiations are in progress. We must be certain that not only the political
[Mr. Graydon.l

and military situations are given due consideration by the powers involved, but also the economics and trade effects of this treaty. That question should be dealt with by the minister during the course of this debate. We would be interested to learn how we fit into the picture so far as any arrangements for peace with Japan are concerned. As the minister well knows, some of the main markets of Japan are now cut off by virtue of Red Chinese domination of the great mainland of China. That in itself raises an obvious question which should not be disregarded in any consideration of a peace treaty with Japan.
I also want to mention another matter which was regarded as of sufficient importance to occupy a place in the report of the external affairs committee. I refer to the recommendation concerning the actions of future Canadian delegations at the general assembly of the United Nations. It is a recommendation with which I am thoroughly in accord. It gained unanimity in the committee, and is worth while mentioning. It reads as follows:
Your committee also recommends that future Canadian delegations to the United Nations general assembly continue to urge that the budgetary contribution which the Soviet union and associated countries make be increased to figures which more closely correspond to their capacities to pay.
As the committee is aware, there has been a scandalous disproportion between other countries and the Soviet union with respect to their assessments and contributions to the cause of peace as represented by the United Nations organization. The budget of the United Nations of course calls for a certain percentage from each country as its share of the upkeep of that organization for the preservation and maintenance of peace. Russia has 180 million people, and Canada 14 million or thereabouts; naturally that disproportion in population causes the raising of eyebrows when we realize that the 180 million people pay a little less than seven per cent of the entire United Nations budget, while Canada, with only 14 million people, pays 3-3 per cent.
I want to commend the delegation from this country for the stand they have taken on this matter. It is not Canada's fault that we have not had a better deal with relation to the Soviet union. I think the standing committee was the place to initiate such a recommendation, and we should tell the United Nations we are not satisfied to allow a nation like the Soviet union, which calls itself a great power and shows all evidence of being a great power, to pay only a little less than seven per cent of the total budget of the whole United Nations organization. A country that can boast of 178 armed

divisions and 30,000 aeroplanes, all poised for any eventuality of war, is not a nation that should be arguing that it should make a small contribution to this organization which would preserve peace. It does not make sense.
In addition, I think attention should be drawn to the fact that if the contribution is determined on the basis of the amount expended for war, then the Soviet union should make a corresponding contribution in the interests of peace. To some extent at least that would balance their activities in the international field. Moreover, they should pay more to the United Nations because they do more to sabotage that organization, and it seems to me there is no justification for the present arrangement.
I was amazed, as I suppose everyone in Canada was, at the last meeting of the United Nations to find a huge budget for the rehabilitation of Korea. That was somewhat premature, as events have developed; nevertheless something like $350 million was being set aside for that purpose, a committee was being set up, and all arrangements were being made under which we would play our part together with the other peace-loving nations in rehabilitating that war-stricken country. But of that $350 million the Soviet union were not putting up a single cent, nor was there any suggestion that they should put up any money. In other words, the people who were not to blame for the Korean problem were having to pay for the intervention of other people.
The whole picture is sordid; but by concurring in that part of the report we will tell the world that Canada is not satisfied with the way the Soviet union is meeting its obligations. It is bad enough to have them disturbing world peace as they are, without our having to pay more as our share of the cost of maintaining it. That, in simple terms, is what I wish to convey to the house-to say how strongly I endorse that part of the committee's report.
In addition I wanted to make one or two references to the recommendation with respect to the international service of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. On this subject some evidence was adduced, though perhaps not as much as the committee might have liked. This question, of course, has a dual significance, and the matter may be said to be under dual jurisdiction. Some of these recommendations might have gone further had it not been for the fact that the committee was anxious not to tread upon the toes of another committee which might be dealing with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which of course has jurisdiction over the international service. Nevertheless
Supply-External Affairs it was made crystal clear that for geographical reasons, with the international service in Montreal and the external affairs department in Ottawa, questions of clearance concerning policy, details and the programs beamed to these other countries make for an unmanageable situation. That was one reason why we in the committee felt we could not go further than simply to call for closer liaison between the department and the international service with respect to policy.
However, I think most committee members have come to the conclusion that we have reached the end of the era of just trying to speak to our free-power friends through the international service. I believe the day has come when we must change our approach and try to reach some of those behind the famous iron curtain who may wish to become our friends. We are told by those who ought to know that there are millions upon millions of prospective listeners in those countries, behind the border between freedom and slavery, who are anxious to hear the message from this country, and there is a very good reason why Canada is in perhaps a much better position than any other nation in the world to speak to those people. We are not suspect as being a great power. We are not suspect as having any international axe to grind. Our reputation and prestige as a people are high, and for those reasons a message from this country would carry more weight.
I was amazed to find that only a very small percentage of our broadcasts is directed to those people. For instance, no broadcasts at all are being beamed to that great section of the Soviet union known as the Ukraine, though some of the most democratic and freedom-loving Ukrainians in the world are to be found in Canada. I mention that to suggest that the percentage of our shortwave broadcasts beamed to countries behind the iron curtain should be increased, and our whole approach to this question changed in view of the fact that we are in the twilight stage between peace and war. No longer can we be said to be in a definite period of peace. I had not intended to elaborate on that point, but I did want to suggest that there is a need, perhaps not for additional facilities, but for a change in the use of the present facilities.
Then I wanted to mention a matter having to do with questions of unanimity and unity at top levels among the major free powers. I suppose nothing has disturbed our people more than the fact that from time to time there have been superficial difficulties, particularly between the United Kingdom and the United States, at high international levels.

Supply-External Affairs I have heard it suggested from time to time, as indeed it was suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North during a debate in this house on a resolution which was later withdrawn, that consideration should be given the setting up of an Atlantic union. I believe most people understand my views in that respect. I think the objective is good; but I agree with what the minister said during that debate, that there is a time and season for all things, and I am not at all sure we have arrived at either the time or the season to proceed along those lines. I do agree that it is an objective we must always keep in view, to which this generation may properly look as a plan for the future.
I have been greatly impressed, as I think every member of this committee must have been-and particularly my learned colleague from Lake Centre-with the fact that at its various meetings the commonwealth parliamentary association has done an immense amount of good in acting as a clearing house for the exchange of views not only among governments but among those who have been elected to office, regardless of their political opinions. That is one of the great advantages of the commonwealth parliamentary association, and I believe those advantages are being realized more and more as the years go by. I believe there is a need for an expansion of that type of endeavour. I throw out this suggestion to the committee:	I am wondering if we should not have, as an experiment, some kind of informal meeting of representatives of the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States, in which there could be frequent clearances of opinions as between men and women of the various political parties who have been elected to the parliaments of those countries. I am not so sure that that would not result in our finding some common denominator for understanding between the peoples of these nations.
It seems to me it is not good enough always to have governments meeting and deciding things, because all governments are not like this one in that they have not such a large majority in the legislature. A good example of this is found in the congress of the United States, and in the slim majority of the Attlee government in Britain. These are factors which might properly be considered. Personally, I should like to see some move made whereby selected representatives from this parliament, from the congress of the United States and the parliament of the United Kingdom, could get together in frequent meetings something similar to that of the commonwealth parliamentary association- not anything in the nature of a strait-jacket organization, but simply with a view to having informal discussions from time to time


for the purpose of clearing up misunderstandings which arise between the peoples of those countries. There would be the additional advantage that the representatives would bring back to their respective legislative bodies, just as they do from the commonwealth parliamentary association, an appreciation of the other person's point of view, which is essential if the free peoples of the world are to march together in common understanding and with common objectives. It is only a personal proposal that I put forward, but I suggest that it is at least worthy of consideration. *
I wish to refer now to a project which has been approved by every political party in Canada. It has been approved by governments, and it has been endorsed by the party to which I have the honour to belong. It has not yet, however, been the subject of the action which I believe should be taken. I should like to have seen in the report of the external affairs committee some recommendation in connection with the St. Lawrence waterway. Such a reference would have afforded the committee, for the first time since the agreement was made in 1941, an opportunity to discuss the matter and record its position. I believe this should have been done some time ago. The agreement was made on March 19, 1941. So far as Canada is concerned, the treaty that was signed at that time, and endorsed by the government, is awaiting approval by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States.
In 1895 the first move with respect to this matter was made when the United States and Canada set up a committee of inquiry. In 1932 the St. Lawrence deep waterway treaty was signed by both countries, but it failed to achieve a two-thirds majority in the United States Senate, so the matter was dropped again. In 1941 the St. Lawrence basin agreement was entered into. At the instance of the United States Senate some changes were made in it in 1949 in order to make it more acceptable to both countries.
In order to show how this matter comes within the purview of the Department of External Affairs, I might say that in between those periods the permanent joint board of defence for Canada and the United States more than once urged that this waterway ought to be completed as a defence measure. From the strait of Belle isle to the lakehead cities of Fort William and Port Arthur is a distance by water of 2,225 miles. It is perhaps the most important inland waterway in the whole world, yet in between those points there is a forty-mile bottleneck which ought to be removed. In this enlightened day and age, when the needs of trade and

commerce, defence and power are all calling for the removal of that bottleneck, it does not make sense that we should delay the construction of this short protected route through the heart of a continent. There is a need for it in time of war as well as in time of peace, particularly in view of the high transshipment costs which the present undeepened waterway causes.
So far as my own part of the country is concerned we are perhaps more keenly interested in this project than some other parts of Canada. For that reason I hesitate to speak on behalf of anyone else in connection with it. On behalf of my part of the province of Ontario I want to say that we have enough power to care for our needs up to the end of 1956. Beyond that we are faced with a bottleneck so far as power is concerned, unless the 1,100,000 horsepower available in connection with the St. Lawrence river project are brought into being. In that forty miles there are 2,200,000 horsepower available to both countries. In addition to that, farther up the waterway there is another estimated two and a quarter million horsepower, but nothing has been planned yet with respect to its development.
This problem was emphasized by a recent visit to the Canadian international trade fair by representatives of the great lakes states bordering this country. Of course, they are interested in the project just as we are. They are just as much concerned as we- are about the lobby which is going on now in congress. They point out that the Mesabi iron range in the state of Minnesota is rapidly petering out and that the ore which normally would come from there is being depleted. That situation, of course, creates a special need, in time of defence preparations, for the necessary raw material which is available in Canada from time to time but which needs a waterway for its transportation. Representatives of Ohio, Michigan, Illinois, Wisconsin and Minnesota have not only expressed their great anxiety, just as we have done, for a movement towards the St. Lawrence waterway development on a basis of immediate urgency, but have welcomed Canada's challenge to build this waterway alone.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that these states are so anxious-as we are-to have the waterway built that some discussion has taken place in their various legislatures or among their state officials with regard to finding some way, under international law, by which they could assume some portion of the cost of a joint undertaking. I want to say this-and when I do so, I speak personally; but as a matter of fact all the
Supply-External Affairs party platforms have called for a joint undertaking of the St. Lawrence development. Frankly, sir, I think that perhaps in the end the best thing that could happen to Canada and to Canadians would be for us to start now to build the St. Lawrence seaway on our own. There are a great number of reasons why that should be done. More than that, even if the present congressional committee makes a favourable decision-and there seems to be a good deal of doubt as to its decision-and recommends a joint undertaking on the St. Lawrence deep waterway, our experience has shown-and perhaps it is indicated in our own parliament as well- that there are a great many ways in which congressional delays can occur. Once that committee has endorsed the undertaking, some other committee or some other body through which it must go for final ratification and approval can block it in its course. One of our real problems is this:	Are we now
running into a long period of indecision from which Canadians may find it difficult to extricate themselves? Americans may say:	Of
course we are studying the matter, and we are still dealing with it; while we are still dealing with it Canadians would, of course not want to make any move with regard to it.

As my hon. friend says, it is here to stay. The government of the China of the future might not have the same attributes as the government of the China of today, but at least the revolution has occurred; the revolutionary government is in power and is going to remain in power. The future of the world depends very largely upon the manner in which we can bring about a better understanding between the revolutionary government of China-and the governments that will follow it, arising out of this revolution-and the democratic world. It was with a good deal of misgiving that one read in the newspapers this morning and heard over the radio last night of the proposal for the signing of a peace treaty to which a government of China later on will be invited to attach its signature, and, as I understand the proposal to be, to co-operate in the terms of the treaty.

There is no question in my mind that Chiang Kai-shek and the group of reactionaries, as they have been described by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, are permanently eliminated as a factor in China. Any attempt to restore that government on the mainland of China will be, I believe, a tragedy for Asia and a tragedy for the world. We know pretty well the opinions of most members of the commonwealth of nations, including India and Pakistan. While Burma is outside the commonwealth, we hope that country will remain on the friendliest of relations with the commonwealth; and we know what their views are on this matter.
I do not know what part has been taken by the Department of External Affairs, the government or the minister in regard to these discussions; but I ask the minister very pointedly if he will indicate exactly what is the position of Canada and the policy of the government in regard to this agreement that is reported to have been made between the United Kingdom and the United States.
After all, we are a Pacific nation. Our borders are washed by the Pacific ocean on the west, and we cannot be negligent of or oblivious to what happens in the Pacific area. It would be well for the minister to tell the House of Commons and the country categorically just where we stand in connection with this matter, involving, as it does, what may be a fateful agreement or understanding.
I want to see communism stopped everywhere. I believe that totalitarian communism menaces the world, but I also believe that if we adopt policies that throw great masses of the people, whether because of their poverty and misery and want or because of situations similar to those in China today, into the orbit of the Soviet union, we are bringing about a situation which will mean a third world war and, in all probability, the destruction of the type of civilization to which we aspire. Certainly it will restrict the freedom we all wish so wholeheartedly to expand.
I know of no announcement in recent weeks that has caused me so much disturbance as the announcement made last night and repeated in the newspapers this morning. We were happy indeed when it seemed that the United States, in removing MacArthur, was endeavouring to reach the point where a negotiated settlement of the Korean conflict could be achieved.
China has unlimited manpower, and the suggestion that we can fight her successfully, that we can bomb her cities, and so on, into submission, seems to me to be quite unrealistic. With her manpower and resources she would ultimately swallow the forces

Mr. Dulles has consulted with our representative in Washington and our representative in Tokyo. I was in Washington yesterday and had a discussion with the assistant secretary of state in charge of Far Eastern affairs. There was an official discussion in Washington between United States, United Kingdom and Canadian officials a few weeks ago, which discussions were resumed in Ottawa a few days after they had finished in Washington. This question has also been discussed in London. I think it is true to say that we have been kept informed and have played a reasonably active part in the negotiations leading up to the present position.
In the early days of these negotiations a draft was circulated by the' United States to the governments more particularly concerned. We made comments on that draft on May 1 and May 21 and gave our views in some detail on every single clause. Having received'the United States draft, at that time the United Kingdom made certain counterproposals of its own, and we also made known in London our views on those counterproposals. In recent days there have been discussions in London between Mr. Dulles and the United Kingdom government designed to remove the differences which had developed in the preliminary discussions between the United States and the United Kingdom approaches to certain of these questions. Those discussions have resulted in an almost complete measure of agreement between London and Washington, and I understand that as a result a combined United States-United Kingdom draft will now be submitted to the other governments concerned for their observations. Once those observations are received it is hoped that a peace treaty may then be speedily concluded.
I am in some difficulty in making known at this particular time our final views in respect of the agreement, if it is a formal agreement, reached in London. We have not yet received any final text of the discussions in London, and I do not think it would be wise for me to express any final view in regard to this matter until that text is received. Of course the committee and parliament know that there have been one or two contentious points in these discussions. They have been mentioned here this morning. One concerns the association of China with the peace treaty, and the other is the disposition of the island of Formosa.
Our position in regard to the former is that this question of Chinese signature on a

Japanese peace treaty should be postponed without prejudice- to any eventual solution. I think the reason for that is obvious. I think it is known to all members of the committee that the United States has recognized one Chinese government while the United Kingdom has recognized another Chinese government. Obviously it would be difficult indeed for them to agree at this time on a Chinese signature to a formal Japanese treaty. Therefore this device has been adopted which I presume will result in a postponement of this issue for the time being, I hope without prejudice to a final and satisfactory solution.
Similarly, with regard to the question of Formosa I think we are all agreed that Japanese sovereignty in Formosa must be brought to an end. I have no doubt that that will be done in the peace treaty. I think it is also pretty clear that the eventual disposition of Formosa cannot be made in any draft treaty at this time. I do not think I can say anything more at this time on this matter.
There were one or two other points that were raised in connection with the proposed Japanese treaty. The hon. member for Peel called attention to the difficulty that we had had in pre-war times in trading with Japan, and stated that he hoped the treaty would take those difficulties into consideration. I can assure him that we have been much alive to the problem. We realize that in pre-war times there were certain difficulties in regard to Japanese trade, and I hope that the treaty will make that situation easier in the future. We have been particularly interested in the fisheries clauses of the treaty. In order to discuss those clauses the Minister of Fisheries, accompanied by some of his officials, visited Washington to take up the matter there with the United States and United Kingdom people. We hope that as a result the fisheries clauses of the treaty will be satisfactory to Canada.

Last evening when the house was in committee of supply a sordid story of a disgraceful international episode was revealed, reminiscent of the dark days of the middle ages when fortresses were betrayed and commanders were sold for a bag of gold. A few years ago the Canadian government underwrote the sale of some seven ships to the nationalist government of China. I understand the loan was jointly guaranteed by the then government of China and the Canadian government. Those seven ships were operating in Chinese waters until the fall of the nationalist government. At that time the banks and other interests concerned became somewhat alarmed as to whether the Canadian shipyards wotild ever be paid for those vessels.
We learned last night that the Canadian government then took back those ships under Canadian registry and the Canadian flag. Since then the payments have been made to
Supply-External Affairs the banks because of the fact that some of those ships have carried on a disgraceful trade between the British port of Hong Kong and the communist ports on the mainland of China. We were told last night that two of the ships have been captured and taken over by the communists. Those ships were operating up the Yangtze river; but the other five ships were still permitted to ply between Hong Kong and the communist ports on the south coast of China. Apparently the communists are making no attempt whatever to seize the other five ships. No doubt the two ships on the Yangtze were seized because if they had left the mouth of the river and gone across the sea of Formosa the United States naval vessels blockading the entrance to the Yangtze river might have seized them, and they would not have been able to bring to China the commodities they were carrying in their cargoes. But no attempt was made to seize those other vessels which are operated by the Ming Sung Industrial Company, because, had they seized the vessels in the communist port, obviously they would not have been able to enter Hong Kong and take again and again to the communist ports the materials which the communists were so anxious to obtain. Eyewitnesses in Hong Kong report that essential war materials are daily included in those cargoes carried by those ships of Canadian registry and flying the Canadian flag. This happens at a time when Canadian destroyers are in the China seas; when Canadian men are fighting in Korea for democracy and are opposed by Chinese formations helping the North Koreans; at a time when not many miles away from these ports of southern China, Canadian missionary nuns have been imprisoned without just cause and have been submitted to treatment which comes quite close to being torture.
When I asked questions as to the nature of the cargo which was being carried, the Minister of Trade and Commerce informed this committee that he could not say whether the ships were carrying contraband on their trips to Canton and up the Yangtze river, but he hoped that they were not. If they were, he did not know what could be done about it. I suggest to the minister, through you, that the Canadian people expect this government will do something about it, and do it without any further delay.
I received my information direct from Hong Kong in a letter dated June 4, 1951, and sent to me personally by the general secretary of the China coast navigating and engineer officers guild. This is an organization of merchant marine officers sailing the China seas. It is a responsible organization. The

Then there is the larger and human aspect: Canadian (?) vessels carrying war materials to Red China to murder Canadian soldiers who espouse the democratic cause and risk their lives for love of country.
The points we desire to emphasize in order to arouse public interest are the following:
1.	The vessels of the Ming Sung Industrial Company (of Canada) are at the time of writing employed in the following trades:	Hong Kong-

Mr. Chairman, I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs will retain his usual composure. It is not a matter of curiosity. We are dealing with a statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I would hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs does support the proposition we have had put forward so frequently, that the statements of the Minister of Trade and Commerce are to be taken seriously.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock. Mr. Diefenbaker: I had intended to make some general remarks with regard to the subject before the committee, and I hope to do this a little later on. What happened just before the luncheon recess aroused my curiosity, and there are a number of questions 
I should like to ask the responsible ministers of the crown in connection with the remarkable conditions revealed by the hon. member for Nanaimo when he read from a letter which he had received some days ago. The more one considers the answers given by ministers, the more one wonders just what are the facts.
Last evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with his knowledge of matters that affect all departments, went into considerable detail in connection with this curious situation which has arisen as a result of the use made of ships bearing the Canadian ensign and sailing in waters that are certainly not friendly. One cannot say that they are enemy waters; for what is taking place in Korea is not war, but rather the punishment of an international aggressor by the combined conscience of mankind.
This is a curious situation, and one which cannot be answered merely by brushing aside what has been said and making the general observation that when the facts are made available and when the government finally speaks, everything will be proper and everyone will be satisfied. Either the minister has the facts, in which case he can say that the letter read by the hon. member for Nanaimo is not correct, or he has not the facts and is merely drawing upon the hope that when the facts are available there will not be a great deal of foundation to the allegations contained in the letter read by the hon. member for Nanaimo.
Last evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave some information. The interesting thing in connection with this matter is that both ministers who have spoken have begun to make excuses. The attitude of the minister of external affairs was that he did not know anything about this until about a week ago. I think the letter was dated June 4. Last evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated that he knew quite a bit about it, but apparently he was glad that he did not know as much as what he was asked to give information on; for he is reported on page 4125 of Hansard, speaking about these ships, as saying:
And they are not my problem, I should say. I had nothing to do with them, except that when they got into difficulty I was called in to try to straighten out the trouble. But they have nothing to do with my department, I am happy to say.
A little later the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra made a suggestion with regard to the mortgages, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce replied as follows:
It might not be the right thing to do. The Department of External Affairs and the Department of Finance are struggling with the situation. I should not be talking about it at all, because I know very little about it, and1 I have nothing to do with it.

iou see the tremendous struggle that is taking place as to who has the responsibility and what are the facts. The Minister of Trade and Commerce went into details, as he usually does, but this was one time when he said that he had nothing to do with the thing at all, that it was a matter in which the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Finance were engaged in a tremendous struggle. What is all the struggle about? Why all the struggle in this matter? If the facts are known, let us know them.
I am going to ask a number of questions of the minister of external affairs arising out of the glimpse given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce last evening. Last evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave a number of facts, but apparently in this struggle the minister of external affairs does not know all the facts that were known to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I want to get some information from the minister of external affairs in regard to this matter. I read what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said last evening, and I shall now ask a number of questions. The answers are there, because the Minister of Trade and Commerce made it clear last evening.
Who were the two or three Canadian shipyards with which the Ming Sung Company made agreements? On what dates were those agreements made? What was the amount of indebtedness that was guaranteed by the government of Canada in reference to the sale of these ships to the Chinese government or the guarantee by the Chinese government? Who were the banks who started to worry? Last evening the minister said, as reported on page 4124 of Hansard:
All went well until the Chinese government, the government of Chiang Kai-shek, fell, and then the banks began to worry a little about their loan. In the uncertain situation that followed, it seemed wise to transfer the ships to the Canadian flag, which was done at the request of the Ming Sung Company, which expressed a desire to protect their loans in Canada.
Who were the banks? What were they worrying about? How much were they worrying about? This could be cleared up if the minister would just produce the correspondence with the Ming Sung Company which revealed the desire of that company to protect their loan.
Then we go on from there and we find that the minister said:
Whether the ships are carrying contraband in their trips to Canton and up the Yangtze river I cannot say. I hope they are not.
A little later last evening the minister did say that he was assured that they were not by someone in Hong Kong. Yesterday one minister of the crown did not know whether
Supply-External Affairs these ships were carrying contraband. He hoped they were not. Today a minister with less information is able to say that they were not. Was that information received within the last twenty-four hours, since the matter was brought before the house? A little further on the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
But the government has no direct interest in the situation other than that they are guarantor to a Canadian bank for part of the money that built the ships for the Ming Sung Company.
Further on the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
When the flag was transferred the ships were exempted from the shipping regulations which required them to be officered by Canadians.
When did this take place? Has this ever been done in other cases? Has a special regulation ever been passed before to permit ships under Canadian registry or flying the Canadian ensign to operate, if not in hostile waters, certainly not in friendly waters?
The minister went on to say:
When they came back under the Canadian flag they were exempted from the requirements.
The question that must be answered for the Canadian people is why that was done. What purpose was there in having these ships flying the Canadian flag under Canadian registry, and exempted from the regulations and requirements applying to Canadian shipping waters as long as they operated in Chinese waters? This cannot be answered by merely expressing the pious hope that some time when the information is available it will be given, and that when it is given it will be information that will be acceptable. This information is available. Remember that the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that one of the two departments having the information, the Department of External Affairs, was struggling with the Department of Finance to find a solution to this matter. When was the order in council passed to do what is most unusual, namely, to allow the Canadian flag to be flown on a ship that is not subject to the Canada Shipping Act? When the minister replies I ask him to say whether this was done by regulation; because he has brought another department into the struggle.
Last night the Minister of Trade and Commerce mentioned only the Department of Finance and the Department of External Affairs, but this morning the Secretary of State for External Affairs brought the Department of Transport into it; so that is another department. Of course they are not engaged in the struggle, because the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not mention them last evening.

The minister may have his explanation available now. The one he gave this morning was not in keeping with that given last evening by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and was one that will far from satisfy anyone, regardless of political persuasion, that all is well when in June of 1951, with the Korean situation what it was, the

I should like to ask the
minister just two questions in this regard. During the last war the false flag device was used extensively. When the United States was still neutral and the neutrality act still in force there was a desire on the part of many United States shipping interests to help the cause of Great Britain. They re-registered a great number of their ships under the Panamanian flag. This was purely and simply a device to get around, not only international law but the United States law which had been passed specifically to prevent trading with any belligerent.
I suggest that the reason these ships are under Canadian registry is the same as that which caused United States ships to be placed under Panamanian registry during a certain period of the last war. That reason was simply to carry on trade which would be illegal flying the flag of the nationals who were running the ships. On the evidence we have heard and on the facts as admitted this trade must be carried out under the protection of the Canadian flag. To carry it out under the flag of communist China, of nationalist China or of any other country would be dangerous and undesirable in some ways. The use of a false flag is well known. Every rumrunner and contraband runner has used it from time immemorial. It is a shock that the Canadian flag should be used in this way.
The cargoes leaving Hong Kong on these ships can be screened; they may be essential foodstuffs or other materials not on the contraband list, but once a ship has cleared Hong Kong there is nothing to prevent it visiting a neutral port such as Portuguese Macao and picking up contraband material and then running along the coast, almost in the protection of the coastal waters, to a communist port. I do not say that that has happened, but that is the sort of thing that the old pirates used to do along the China coast. Coastal waters are particularly difficult to search. For many years the running of arms up and down the China coast reached tremendous proportions. During the civil war in China ships had to be specially protected to prevent seizure when avelling along the China coast by means of grille work to separate the crew from the passengers and prevent the passengers seizing the ship. If we have finished with this Ming Sung business I should like to refer to the question of the peace treaty with Japan. I agree with those who have said that it is just as well to get this treaty signed and sealed, even though the circumstances may be somewhat unsatisfactory. We have reached the stage where, if it is to be done at all, it should be done quickly. Obviously the position of Russia is the same old argument disguised in different words, and if we should accept their views we would find ourselves in the same mess we have in Europe. It is quite obvious that certain basic differences between the United Kingdom and the United States have not been removed, but a very interesting formula has been adopted under which there is an apparent compromise. I cannot recall a case in recorded history, however, in which a defeated country has been able to name the government with which it will negotiate a peace treaty. That is a precedent which offers some very interesting possibilities.
I have just a word to say on the situation in Japan itself and what may be the effect of a peace treaty. Some time ago a well known general said that what had happened to Japan was the greatest reformation recorded in modern history. I may have some regard for the military ability of that general, but I have not very much regard for his political sagacity. He has fallen into the error common to many of us. We simply cannot take our democratic customs and habits and impose them upon other peple in a matter of a few short years. We can make no greater blunder than to believe we can do that. What has happened is that in Japan today there is a veneer of democracy. I am certain the situation, is better than it was under the authoritarian state of 1939, but I am quite sure that once Japan regains her sovereignty even such measure of democracy as she has now will be appreciably lessened.
The question which interests me is this. There are in Japan at this moment about six million workers organized in trade unions, with more or less the same rights which we accept as normal in this country. The indications now are that many of these rights will be taken away, and many of the democratic practices which have been thrust upon the Japanese will disappear once that treaty is

Supply-External Affairs signed. I should like to know whether the treaty contains any safeguard to assure that at least some of these rights will be retained by the Japanese.

speechtext: May I ask a question with regard to the point four program? It is referred to as the Truman point four program. I have always been a little bit confused in my own mind whether this point four program is really run by the United States government or by the United Nations, or really what the arrangement is in connection with it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: WEIGHING AND MEASURING DEVICES, ETC.- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is true that this United Nations program is sometimes referred to as the point four program and that the expression was taken from a statement of the President of the United States in a message to congress in which he dealt with this subject. It is a United States expression, if I may put it that way, which has been taken over by others. The point four program is much more than a United States enterprise. It is quite true that the United States is bearing or will bear the brunt of the financial burden in this matter. That is obvious. But it is also true the operation of the United Nations program will be controlled by the United Nations, or by a special committee of the United Nations which incidentally is under the direction of a former Canadian civil servant.

subsubtopic: WEIGHING AND MEASURING DEVICES, ETC.- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: What I was trying to find out was this. We are contributing to the Colombo plan under the commonwealth arrangements. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: WEIGHING AND MEASURING DEVICES, ETC.- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: Well, I can understand the hon. member's confusion in the matter, because of the confusion connected with the indiscriminate use of the expression "point four". Mr. Chairman, I think this would be the item under which a person could make a few observations concerning the Colombo plan, particularly in view of the fact that this vote covers technological and other assistance being given in southeast Asia.
i A number of members from the House of Commons, along with Senator Roebuck from the other place, in the months of November and December attended a parliamentary conference in Wellington, New Zealand, and Canberra, Australia, at which there were also representatives from the United States in the persons of two United States senators, namely Senator Ferguson from Michigan and Senator Green from Rhode Island. There were also representatives at this parliamentary conference from India and other parts of Asia. I am sure all hon. members of the House of Commons who were present at the conference will agree that the one message we were asked to bring back to our respective parliaments was the need for assistance to India of the kind contemplated under this item,
Supply-External Affairs and also generally under the Colombo pian, before communism achieves its intention of subjugating that land of India.
I believe one of the best booklets I have seen on the subject, indeed the only one issued as yet from the commonwealth parliamentary association meeting, is in the form of a report to the United States Senate, which I now hold in my hand. This was presented by Senator Green on March 22, to that legislative body. In this booklet is set forth something of what took place at that commonwealth parliamentary conference, and the ideas expressed there, unofficial though they were, from all parts of the commonwealth.
This morning the hon. member for Peel mentioned how helpful it would be if a conference of unofficial persons, representative of the various parts of the commonwealth arid the United States, could be convened. The minister offered his opinion regarding that suggestion. As a matter of fact there has been such a body in existence, although unofficially, since 1943, at which time, and for the first time, representatives of the United States congress, both from the Senate and the House of Representatives, met here in Ottawa. Since that time there have been a number of meetings.
At the conference in Australia there were representatives from the United States Senate in attendance. While there were disagreements in regard to courses which should be followed by several nations, without exception every Asiatic representative made an appeal to the representatives at the commonwealth parliamentary conference to stress the absolute need that something be done by way of assistance in southeast Asia. That was the view expressed by members of the legislative councils from Singapore, Malaya, India and Ceylon. Without exception they stressed the need of something being done immediately along that line. I should like to quote a few words from the report made to the United States Senate to which I have made reference, as follows:
India's basic requirements for improving the standard of living there must comprise the development of irrigation, schemes and rural electrification. Agricultural production must be increased; India needs more fertilizers as also agricultural machinery and building materials, and she must try to find them at a reasonable cost.
Then there is this significant statement:
The United States has an important stake in the Middle East. If 350,000,000 Indians should come under the domination of communism, the free world will virtually be split in half. Many think that as an integral phase of our global planning we must assist India to remain outside the communist orbit -must do this before it is too late and without strings attached.

That was the view, not only of the commonwealth representatives outside India and the United States representative who were there, it was stressed over and over again by the representatives from India. All of these had at one time or another fought against Britain. As they spoke I thought of the words spoken some years ago by the Secretary of State for External Affairs-I cannot quote them exactly-when speaking of the commonwealth. He referred to those members within the commonwealth who had achieved commonwealth membership by fighting against Britain while the great majority of the member nations concerned had achieved it by fighting with Britain. Without exception, those who had fought against Britain stressed a desire to see the British commonwealth preserved and maintained, without which freedom would never be assured anywhere in the world. In the maintenance of freedom they emphasized the need of support of the plan which was evolved at Colombo whereby millions of dollars in technological materials and other commodities would be provided.
As far as the Colombo plan is concerned, I doubt whether it has been sold to our own people. When I spoke about it on one occasion in this house I received three letters condemning me for supporting a proposition to give assistance to South America. That was the understanding of three correspondents with regard to what the Colombo plan actually comprised. Those letters came from three different parts of the country and there had been no collaboration, but they were all agreed that it was dangerous for Canadians to support a proposition that would bring any degree of assistance to South America.
I bring this matter again to the attention of the minister and re-emphasize the need. I realize that the government of India took a stand against the delivery to that country of low-grade wheat, either by way of state assistance or under the Colombo plan. Even if that assistance might not materially reduce the suffering that is now being endured there, nevertheless, even at this date and before the present year's crop is harvested, something should be done if it is only in the nature of a token gift of a number of hundreds of thousands of bushels of wheat. We would thus give to these people, not only renewed hope but an appreciation of Canadian assistance. Canada has a record of activities and actions, not only as a country as a whole but also its officials in the Department of External Affairs, and is held in very high regard in Asia. The recent gift of the United States

of several hundred thousand tons of wheat has had a tremendous effect on the thinking of the Indian people with regard to the United States, which is sometimes described in Asia as being an imperialist country. Canada is not in the position of being suspect, however unjustified suspicion in that regard may be in regard to the United States.
Whether or not several million bushels of wheat are available, I do feel that the delivery of a few hundred thousand bushels of wheat at this time-it is available in western Canada because the crop has been harvested and threshed this spring-would go a long way today to answer the contention of communism that the capitalist countries will do nothing to preserve Asia, and India in particular, against poverty and starvation.
Asia is in revolt against poverty. Today the Asiatic is being lured toward communism by the promise of material advancement which is held out as a means whereby he can secure support. It may be too late one, two or three years from now. The attitude of the Indian delegation was that they would give support to the United Nations, but when they were asked what contribution they would give in the way of manpower toward the setting up of an international police force to maintain peace or to give assistance in punishing aggression, the answer invariably was that that was something they were opposed to.
Their concept of the United Nations and the support they should give is one of moral assistance and high idealism. Today the government of India is endeavouring to meet the challenge of communism that has overrun southeast Asia to an extent of which we in this country have no appreciation. One weapon that will do more today than any weapon of war is the weapon of food. It is the greatest answer to communism among people whose inalienable destiny has been poverty.
I do not want to reiterate what has been said so often and so well by the hon. member for Peel. With all the force that I can bring to a discussion of this subject I appeal to the minister and to the government of Canada to do something. Do not wait until the fall. Do not ask these people to accept wheat that we would not turn into flour in our own country. Good wheat is available, not in the amount necessary to meet the situation there, but the effect of even a token delivery at this time would1 be far greater than the delivery of many million more bushels of wheat and other assistance six, eight or ten months from now. The booklet to which I have referred sets out the situation as the result of the

thinking of these United States senators on the subject consequent upon attending this conference, and they say:
We found simple, unrealistic, and almost childlike ignorance of the communist danger with nerve centres deadened to the meaning of communism . . . Everywhere in the Far East and in the Near East we saw evidences of shrewd, insidious communist propaganda. It was handled by natives who were won over and in Moscow educated to communism. It exploited every complaint, every hope, every fear, and every condition in each country in order to induce the people to hate America and the west, and to embrace communism.
Almost every one of the representatives at the conference to which I have made reference is a graduate of Oxford or Cambridge, men who have had every opportunity in the occidental world of education and who today are members of their respective parliaments, and their considered opinion was that nothing would better meet the onrush of communism into India than help of an economic nature. Particularly so far as the people of India are concerned, who for all time have been in one of two states, underfed or famished, the greatest answer and antidote to communism would be some assistance economically, even though only a modicum, in order to remove the threat of starvation. It is for that reason that I have said these few words on this occasion, to again enjoin the minister to secure some assistance from the government. The determination has been made to contribute $25 million this year. A part of that $25 million, if delivered in the form of foodstuffs, wheat and the like, will go further to meet the challenge that faces Asia today, as it does all parts of the world, than any other investment that I can think of.

I should like to associate myself with the comments of the horn, member for Lake Centre, and I should like to say a word in support of the general idea of developing the British commonwealth. Far too much attention is being given to the United Nations, the Atlantic pact, and pretty nearly any sort of international organization, compared with the interest shown in the British commonwealth. It seems to me that our generation is not being taught the tremendous value of the British commonwealth. Why that should be I do not know. I hope the minister and all members of his department are enthusiastic about the British commonwealth because enthusiasm is catching. Likewise lack of enthusiasm is also catching.
In Canada there is a tendency on the part of a good many people to think that when one speaks in favour of the British commonwealth one must be an imperialist. That attitude is utter nonsense and indicates
Supply-External Affairs ignorance and prejudice on the part of those who so speak. The British commonwealth is a great international organization. In 1914 the British commonwealth had more power in its little finger with which to preserve the peace of mankind than the United Nations will ever have, and it did not require contributions of money from all members in order to accomplish its end. I maintain if we can restore the British commonwealth to the relative degree of strength that it possessed in 1914 we shall by that action be doing mankind the greatest service it is possible for us to render in these terrible times in which we live.
The British commonwealth can be rebuilt. All that is necessary is that first of all we have an appreciation of what it means, and then that we work together to bring back the financial, industrial, trading and military strength which was the dread of all enemies of freedom for one hundred years up to 1914. If we could only restore the British commonwealth to where it was in 1914 how much more peacefully we could rest in our beds at night. How much more securely we could live. Without wishing to multiply words, may I urge that the minister do everything in his power to rebuild the British commonwealth, not in the sense that any portion thereof should ever lose any degree of its sovereignty. The British commonwealth never was strong because of the power of any central body to coerce members of the commonwealth. Its strength lay in the fact that members of the commonwealth contributed all their means and their blood gladly, cheerfully and happily, being inspired with the great ideal of gaining freedom and security for the world. That is the sort of thing we must have in the members of the commonwealth today. I urge the minister that he spare no effort to restore to the members of the British commonwealth their strength and courage, and faith in themselves.
I do not wish to labour overmuch this one matter that I propose to mention, I have referred to it several times. Most hon. members who were in the house in 1945 will remember the attitude I took on the subject in the fall of that year. I refer to the international monetary fund. In my opinion the international monetary fund is one of the gravest dangers in the world today. I suggest to the minister that he give the most careful study to the evil implications of that organization. I should like to draw to the minister's attention, without going into too much detail, the recommendation of the ECE report for 1950. I believe I will read the comment on this report appearing in the issue of May 29, 1951, of the Christian Science Monitor.

That is quite true. The hon. member did ask a question on the orders of the day, and at that time he was informed that it could be dealt with when my estimates came up. In fairness to him I think I should attempt to answer that question now. The question which would have been raised by the hon. member, I think, concerned the advisability of bringing the federal republic of Germany into closer association with the community of free nations, and making peace with free Germany. I think that is what he had in mind this morning, and I might make a Short statement on that matter which is a question of some importance.
The announcement was made on October 26 last of the intention of the government to terminate the state of war with Germany as soon as we were in a position to do so in concert with our friends and allies. Since that announcement last autumn we have been in constant touch with the progress made both by the occupying powers and the German federal republic on this matter. Before we or the occupying powers could take further action it was necessary for the German federal republic to pass legislation eliminating from its laws all references to the state of war. That was done by the lower house, the Bundestag, on May 30, 1951, and by the upper house as recently as June 8. The promulgation of that German law is expected within a few days.

As soon as the new German law has been promulgated Canada, as well as other countries still technically at war with Germany, will be free to terminate that state of war; and in Canada this will take the form of a proclamation in the Canada Gazette.
I think I should recall here that the announcement of October 26, 1950, to which I have referred, makes it clear that such action will be quite different from any formal peace settlement with Germany. It will in no way affect Germany's obligations in respect of such matters as debts, claims and all that sort of thing. In order that the termination of the state of war may be related as closely as possible to similar action by the occupying powers, we are in consultation with London, Paris and Washington as to their intentions as soon as the Germans have taken their action. In any event it would appear that the necessary legislation will have been passed by the west German government before the end of June, so it is only a question of days, I should think, before Canada would be in a position to terminate the state of war with Germany.

I think it is important that we find out, during this debate, just what was contained in that cabinet directive. It seems to be a most unusual course to be followed, both by the minister arid the government. This section to which the minister referred was never intended to meet a case of this kind. Section 133A of the act reads as follows:
The minister may, if he thinks fit, and upon such conditions, if any, as he thinks proper to impose, exempt any ship-
It does not say anything about exempting seven ships.
-from any requirement contained in sections one hundred and thirteen, one hundred and fourteen, one hundred and thirty-two and one hundred and thirty-three, or dispense with the observance of any such requirement in the case of any ship,-
And I would point out these words:
-if he is satisfied that that requirement has been substantially complied with in the case of that ship, or that compliance with the requirement is unnecessary in the circumstances of the case, and that the action taken or provision made as respects the subject matter of the requirement in the case of the ship is as effective as actual compliance with the requirement.
The hon. member for Lake Centre will deal with clause 2 of this section but clause 1 is meant to cover only a case where it is not necessary to comply fully with the terms of these particular sections of the Canada Shipping Act. It was never intended to be used as a blanket measure to enable the citizens of another country to get the protection of the Canadian flag. In going that far the minister has stretched the section of the Canada Shipping Act far beyond any intention that was in the mind of parliament when this section was enacted.
He has said that these seven ships needed the protection of the Canadian flag and therefore this blanket exemption was granted.
Supply-External Affairs I would ask him to explain to the committee what right a company operated by Chinese citizens had to come to the Canadian government and get the protection of the Canadian flag? He has also made it clear that the banks had a mortgage or mortgages on these ships. Why was it necessary for the government to step in under those conditions? The situation is much worse than we were told it was earlier in the day. Apparently it was not a case of trying to protect the liability under the guarantee which had been given by the government. Here you have, in effect, a case of protecting the banks.

We understood from the Minister of Trade and Commerce last night that they no longer were in that category. I would ask the Minister of Transport to explain whether the two ships that are up the Yangtze river are still registered as Canadian ships. I would also ask him to explain what control, if any, the Canadian government now has over these ships.
The one exemption to which he has referred had to do with the officers or with certain members of the crew. What control has the Canadian government today over these ships? Furthermore, what steps would have to be taken to withdraw flag rights from these ships? Certainly it would appear to me to be a case where the flag rights should be withdrawn without further delay. I would ask the Minister of Transport to say what steps would have to be taken to bring that situation about.

With reference to our conversation this morning regarding a letter from the China Coast Navigating and Engineer Officers Guild dated June 4, 1951, I wish to present a number of facts which may throw light upon the misleading statements made by the said letter.
Our vessels in trade: Hong Kong-Macao, passenger and cargo; Hong Kong-Macao-Canton, passenger and cargo; Hong Kong-Canton, passenger only; Hong Kong-Canton (nonscheduled service); oversea Chinese sent back to China from Malaya and Indonesia and sometimes cargo.
All cargoes shipped by our vessels are cleared by Hong Kong government in similar manner as cargoes shipped by other company's vessels. We do not enjoy special facility nor are we the only shipping company in Hong Kong-Canton trade. All our trades are legitimate.
Our officers and crew are all Chinese under the exemption from merchant shipping ordinance granted by the Hong Kong government. No Russian captain or officer, or crew on our ships.
Ships in China may be required to handle any kind of transportation, but that has nothing to do with our Canadian ships in Hong Kong.
To the contrary, regulations under the said exemption have been strictly complied with by our company.
As the main accusation made by the Guild's letter is the carriage of war materials, we beg that you would give us the honour of inspecting our manifests of cargoes carried wherever you please.
One point besides the contents of the Guild's letter is that the bulk of trade between Hong Kong and Canton is handled by the Kowloon Canton Railway, a government enterprise. We are not in a position to say that Hong Kong depends on normal trade with China, but we are definite that our Canadian ships in Hong Kong would not be able to earn their direct upkeep if normal trade is denied them.

Before that committee a representative of the city of Vancouver opposed the passage of the bill on two grounds. In the first place it was contended that the increase sought, namely, $50 million, was excessive. In the second place the city of Vancouver has become convinced, as the result of experience before the board of transport commissioners on a recent application for an increase in telephone rates, that there are unfair contracts between this telephone company and its affiliates under which the telephone company is charged an unfair amount for certain services, and in turn passes on that excessive charge to the telephone users.
I propose to speak very briefly this evening on these two grounds of objection raised on behalf of the great city of Vancouver before the standing committee. The main objection to an excessive increase in capital is that the larger the increase the longer the time will be before the telephone company must return again to parliament. This company is incorporated under a charter passed by the dominion parliament. In that charter there is a provision which sets out that its works are for the benefit of Canada. The result of that provision is that the provincial public utilities board has no control whatever over the telephone company. It controls other utilities such as electric light companies, but it has no control whatever over this particular telephone company. The only public bodies which have any control at all are this parliament, when an increase in capital is sought or some other change in the charter, and the board of transport commissioners, which only has authority over the rates charged by the company and over the actual issuing of shares.
The city council have felt that the company has asked for too large an increase. They fear that an increase of $50 million will enable the telephone company to stay away from parliament for fourteen or fifteen years. They have no desire to hold up development or the installation of new telephones. They heartily approve of the development plans of the telephone company and it was admitted before the committee by Mr. Hamilton, the vice-president of the company, that if the amount of the increase were reduced the effect would not be to retard development at all but only that the company would have to come back to parliament at an earlier date than if the full $50 million were granted.

I can best illustrate that objection by pointing out that the British Columbia Telephone Company is owned by a Montreal company known as Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company, which in turn is owned by the Gary group. The Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company in Montreal is purely an investment corporation. It has no staff to do any telephone work, but there is what is known as a licensing contract between that company and the British Columbia Telephone Company which provides that the British Columbia company must pay one per cent of its gross revenue to Anglo-Canadian in return for technical and financial advice. In 1948 the amount paid came to $181,051. At that time the rate was 1J per cent; it was dropped to 1 per cent just before the hearing of the rate application in 1950. Last year, when the British Columbia company had a gross operating revenue of over $16 million it had to pay Anglo-Canadian under this licensing contract more than $160,000 calculated at the rate of 1 per cent.
It is admitted that Anglo-Canadian has no facilities to supply any of these services, but it is argued that the Gary company could supply them. The Gary company had no contract with the British Columbia Telephone Company,, and from Anglo-Canadian in 1948 received only $3,150 for the same services, whereas British Columbia Telephone Company had to pay Anglo-Canadian over $181,000.
