If it were the fact that the essential information was not available I would be the first to concur in the suggestion. In fact I indicated earlier that I thought that if the information was not available the item might at that time stand until it could be obtained. I would point out to the minister, however, that as a result of the further discussion which took place it is now clear that most of the essential information is available. There is one subject on which the government possibly has not yet been able to satisfy itself, and that is as to the present personnel manning the ships. It may be that they have not been able to find out whether in fact a Russian captain is in charge of one of the ships. It is obvious from the letter that was read into the record just before the dinner recess that an inquiry had been directed to that subject and that a reply had been received.
While that is important, and while it would be extremely useful to know if in fact these ships, manned by other than Canadian seamen, are under the direction of Russian captains or officers, nevertheless I suggest that the information that could readily be placed before the house would make it possible for us to settle some of the principles which are now involved in this discussion. It seems to me that the only two things concerning which the government suggests it still requires information are as to the identity of the crews and whether or not the ships are carrying materials of war. There are, however, other things that could be placed before the house which would explain this transaction. There certainly must be files readily available dealing with this particular subject. The matter was placed before the cabinet, as has been explained by the Minister of Transport.
The very fact that it was placed before the cabinet brought to the attention of the
4184	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs Secretary of State for External Affairs the international aspect of this problem. The financial aspects are secondary to the very important principles involved in a change of registry of this kind and the transfer to Canadian registry, with the use of the Canadian flag, of ships operating in association with a company whose main business is now in communist China. It has been explained to us that this was not done by order in council but was done after consultation with the government by government directive. That directive can be placed before the committee. I hope it will not be suggested that, with this discussion having taken place yesterday and today, the government is not in a position to place that directive before the committee. It would indicate exactly what the instructions were.
It also should be possible to obtain information as to the terms of the directive and as to the circumstances under which it was made. The application which prompted a decision of that kind will be on file and would explain the grounds upon which the government made this very unusual decision. Then we also should be informed now as to how it was that the government agreed to the transfer to Canadian registry of ships which had originally been delivered to a company operating mainly in communist China, and why the government concurred in the setting up of a Canadian subsidiary of that Chinese company with head office in Montreal at a time when this company, with branches throughout China, was operating within the communist area.
I should think that would be clearly disclosed by the material which must have been on file at the time this matter was considered and the decision reached by the government. The files would also disclose, and it would be possible for the government to ' produce, the communications which informed this Canadian subsidiary of the Chinese company as to what the conditions and terms were under which they would operate these ships with Canadian flags and under Canadian registry.
Then we come to a later stage. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has already disclosed that this subject has been under consideration for a sufficient length of time to receive a communication from the Canadian representatives in Hong Kong. The letter he read into the record indicated that an inquiry had been directed to the Hong Kong representative of the Ming Sung Company and a reply had been received from that company denying that a Russian officer was in charge of one of the ships, and making certain statements as to the nature of the


freight carried. The very fact that the government directed such an inquiry and that it has already received a reply indicates that there must be some other material that can be disclosed to the house which prompted the inquiry. Doubtless there is other information. The Minister of Trade and Commerce undertook to table the letter from which he read and the covering letter from the Canadian office in Hong Kong, and I trust that those documents have been tabled already for the information of this house.
This would give us a fairly complete picture. It would make it possible for us to see exactly what has happened in this case. It is not possible for us to understand what took place unless that information is fully disclosed. Before dinner the Minister of Transport made a comment to the effect that there was an established practice that government directives of this nature are not produced. I would hope that upon further consideration neither the Minister of Transport nor the Secretary of State for External Affairs would take such a position, because this transaction is of such a nature that the members of this house should have full information. There can be no question of security involved, or anything of that kind, which would present any reason why this house should not be fully informed as to the directive which interpreted this very remarkable decision, which resulted in the transfer of these ships to Canadian registry.
I have outlined these things that could be given the house. This must be information which is readily available now. If the minister who is leading the house, and who has stated the position of the government, will examine the suggestions I have made he will not find one that could not be complied with. Then we would be in a position to discuss this subject which is definitely related in a very important way to the policies of the government in relation to communist China and other communist countries at this time. It is known that the Secretary of State for External Affairs intends to leave Canada within the next few days. This matter involves a very important question of policy. The information I have mentioned can be produced and this whole question of policy can be considered while the minister is still here.
Of course there is one way in which this debate could be disposed of: that would be for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to adopt the suggestion which was made in all earnestness, that the government announce now that it will cancel this transfer and bring these ships back fully under Canadian control. I repeat that suggestion and urge upon

the Minister of Public Works its adoption as a means not only of facilitating the business of the house but of settling something which otherwise is going to cause the people of Canada very great concern.

Mr. Chairman, the
Minister of Public Works mentioned the genesis of this affair, if I heard him aright, and the genesis of it would be the circumstances under which the cabinet directive was made in April, 1950. The exemption of this company from coming within the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act was an act of the Minister of Transport. He is in the house now, and must have in his files all the information that we have requested. Section 133A to which he referred this afternoon provides that the minister may, if he thinks fit, exempt any ship from any requirement referred to therein, if he is satisfied that the requirement has been substantially complied with, and so on.
The minister received a directive from the cabinet. I would have thought that what he did under this act would usually be done under an order in council or regulation. In this case it was not so done. If it had been done by regulation or order in council, that regulation or order in council would have been, under the law, placed before parliament. However, he says he proceeded upon the basis of a directive from the cabinet. He could only proceed on that basis if he was satisfied that the request of this company was a proper one. The information asked for by us must be in the files of the Minister of Transport, upon whose shoulders the responsibility for granting the exemption rests. Who made the application for change of registry? If I understood the Minister of Transport aright, his explanation is not the same in that regard as that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce last evening. What were the circumstances upon which the minister exercised an almost judicial discretion in determining that this company should be exempt from the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act? What was the evidence before him that caused him to make a decision so at variance with what one would expect, allowing aliens, none of whom acknowledge the Canadian flag or anything it stands for, the use of the Canadian flag in China seas.
To whom was money owing in respect of the building of these ships? How did the banks find themselves in a position where some $12 million was owing to them? What were the circumstances in connection with the financing of these ships? How much money did the Minister of Trade and Commerce advance the builders of these ships through the Canadian Commercial Corporation. Those are questions upon which we have a right to

have information. This information must be in the possession of the Minister of Transport for certainly no Minister of Transport would grant an exemption under section 133A on any of the evidence that has so far been placed before parliament today, either by him or by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
This afternoon production of the directive was asked for. The directive must set forth the circumstances explaining why this was done. What is the explanation available to the government in regard to the extraordinary proposition of placing these ships, certainly if not under the control at least under the active surveillance of communists in China? Certainly no one could seriously argue that such extraordinary action would be taken on the kind of evidence that the members of the government have placed before this committee during the past twenty-four hours.
Now then, there is a second phase of it, once we find out the genesis of the circumstances. It might be of interest to know who are the Canadian directors of this subsidiary. Did the banks make any advances to these directors after the exemption order was granted by the Minister of Transport? Did the parent company, the Chinese company, owe the banks? These are questions to which parliament has a right to have answers. These are questions, the information regarding which must be in the possession of the Minister of Transport or he could not .have exercised his discretion in granting the order under section 133A. They must have been put before cabinet. The minister went to the cabinet for advice. What information did he provide the cabinet with? Why was this done? What is the advantage to Canada to have the ships operating under these circumstances? What Canadian wants to see the Canadian flag carried around in the China sea by those who certainly acknowledge nothing of what the flag stands for?

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the answer which I gave to the committee this afternoon is all of the information that I had at my disposal. If the hon. member for Lake Centre is perplexed, I am afraid he is attempting to make a great deal of political capital out of this matter which is not at all as e ctraordinary as he or those associated with him would lead us to believe.

Supply-External Affairs
When I came to the house this afternoon at five o'clock or five-thirty, I asked what the questions were that I was required to answer. The leader of the opposition kindly said, in order not to have those questions repeated, that perhaps I could get them from someone else and obtain the reply. I should like the committee to be reminded of the fact that this is an application which was made in March of 1950. I do not pretend to have a better memory than any other member of parliament, and I certainly cannot be expected to carry in my head or in my mind all of the details concerning this application made more than a year ago. Armed with the questions which were given to me, I obtained the information which was available at the time; and by the time I gave it, it was five minutes to six. It was therefore impossible for me or for any other officers of the department to obtain all the information that was required by the leader of the opposition and by the hon. member for Lake Centre. As a matter of fact, a great deal if not the greater part of the information asked for by the hon. gentleman is not obtainable from my department or from my files. But since both the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Lake Centre have repeated the speeches they made earlier, and added to them, let me repeat what I said at the time and what the position is.
In March of 1950 an application was made for Canadian registry of some seven ships, if my memory serves me aright. The application was made by the Ming Sung Corporation Limited, a foreign company; and out of that it followed that they formed a Canadian subsidiary. It was stated by the leader of the opposition that the government concurred in the formation of the Canadian subsidiary. I am not in a position to say whether it was a provincial corporation or a federal corporation. If it was a provincial corporation, surely the federal government did not concur in its formation. If it was a federal corporation, then it was incorporated in the usual manner through the office of the Secretary of State, and the government had nothing to do with concurrence in that. What the Department of Transport did-and I take the full responsibility for it-was to grant Canadian registry. There was nothing else that could be done because any other company doing the same thing that this company did-that is, form a Canadian subsidiary and get a bill of sale-had every right to go to Vancouver, to Toronto, to Montreal or to Halifax, register that bill of sale and there be entitled to place under Canadian registry the ships in question. There is nothing abnormal in that procedure.


The next thing that happened was the application under section 133A for an exemption from the carrying of British subjects as officers, mates or engineers, not of crews. The leader of the opposition said: You have all of the information required; surely you can tell us what the present personnel is, what the identity of the crew is. I have no way of finding out what is the present personnel of those ships. Neither have I any way of knowing what the identity of the crew is. But what I said this afternoon is that when the application was made for a certificate of exemption under section 133A of the Canada Shipping Act, the names of the officers, mates and engineers of those ships were furnished to us. They were all of Chinese origin, all Chinese nationalists. What happened since then I cannot say. It may be that the Secretary of State for External Affairs can obtain that information. I do not know whether he can or not. But certainly I have no way of obtaining it.
Let me go a step further. The hon. member says that under section 133A this certificate of exemption was granted, something which was a matter of grave responsibility. I consider that those matters coming under section 133A are always serious matters. When I have granted an exemption, as I have done oftentimes but not repeatedly, I have exercised the discretion myself. But on this occasion I felt that I should not do that. On this occasion I felt the circumstances warranted that the matter be revealed to my colleagues in the cabinet. And that I did. And I was given instructions to grant the exemption under 133A, which I did in the month of May or April, of 1950.
Now then, the leader of the opposition says, "Produce the directive." I will have to inquire whether or not a written directive was given. I have no recollection of whether it was or not. I do know this, that repeatedly matters are discussed in cabinet and advice is sought from them-"Here is a matter in which I require advice." A discussion follows and advice is given.
There was no order in council, so far as I could ascertain in the few minutes that were at my disposal this afternoon-about twenty-five minutes. There was no order in council given. There was approval given. And so far as I can recollect-and I might be mistaken; I might have to take it back-but so far as I can recollect there was no written directive. Approval was sought and approval was granted.
That being so, there was an oral directive that exemption be granted. And acting under

that advice, and with the concurrence of my colleagues in the cabinet, I issued the exemption under 133A.
I now come to the main objections that are being raised, both by the leader of the opposition and by the hon. member for Lake Centre, who asked countless questions dealing with other phases of the matter. The financial aspects of this I have had nothing to do with. If I were familiar with them in detail I would give them to the house.
Then it was asked: Who made the application. When was the application made? What were the advantages? I repeat that I have no information of that kind available. But I did put, in the few minutes at my disposal before six o'clock, all the information that I had at my disposal and that I was able to get; and I will say this, that if the House of Commons wishes to have it I can obtain all the information that it is possible for me to get in the department.
Beyond that I cannot go. I have nothing to hide, in so far as the two matters with which I have been concerned in this application, are concerned.

I said in my statement a moment ago that there were a number of exemptions granted under 133A, and they are not granted as matters which are extraordinary.
For instance, I can think, during the postwar period, of a number of exemptions being granted for engineers, mates and so on- second mates acting in the place of first mates, and third engineers in the place of second engineers, because it was impossible to get first class engineers and first class mates. And they were done as a matter of course.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: That has nothing to do with this.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: That is the type of exemption which was contemplated by section 133A.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Not necessarily.
Supply-External Affairs

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Not the wholesale exemption of masters, mates and engineers on seven vessels, obviously.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I noticed the hon. member made that point this afternoon, and he makes it again tonight. I notice that in prior applications under 133A more than one ship has been granted exemption. I cannot give the name from memory, but I know of one case where several applications were made under 133A, and granted at the same time.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Ships in the China sea?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I am dealing with ships in Canadian waters.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Here were ships operating in communist waters. At the time this exemption was granted, last April or May, all that southeast part of China bad been taken over by the communists. These ships obviously were to operate in communist waters, so there was nothing ordinary, I suggest, about the exemptions.
B.ut whatever the case may be with regard to later exemptions, the minister must have granted this exemption in writing, and I would ask that he produce a copy of that formal exemption which was issued to this company.
Last night the Minister of Trade and Commerce discussed that matter, and he is reported at page 4124 of Hansard in this way:
When they came back under the Canadian flag they were exempted from the requirements. This was the most disturbing condition to meet and, rather than let the ships go, which might have been the wisest course, we did take what seemed to be the practical course, to bring the physical ships under the Canadian flag, but to exempt the ships from the requirements of the Canada Shipping Act as long as they operated in Chinese waters.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce there pointed out that this exemption applied only while these ships were in Chinese waters. Surely the Minister of Transport can produce the actual exemption or exemptions containing these various provisions. If that were done it would help us to get rid of the matter.
He also said in the course of his remarks a few moments ago, or at least gave me the impression, that this application for Canadian registry came out of the blue, in the ordinary way that any application would come for registration. But the Minister of Trade and Commerce made some comments on that side of the question, too, last night when he said:
All went well until the Chinese government, the government of Chiang Kai-shek, fell, and then the banks began to worry a little about their loan. In the uncertain situation that followed, it seemed wise-
4190	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs And obviously the minister meant there that it seemed wise to himself and to his
fellow members in the cabinet.
-to transfer the ships to the Canadian flag, which was done at the request of the Ming Sung Company, which expressed a desire to protect their loans in Canada.
Now, this whole question obviously was considered by the cabinet a year ago. Can either of the ministers, either the Minister of Transport or the Secretary of State for External Affairs, tell us why it was that this protection of the Canadian flag was given to these ships? One or other of those ministers must know why it was that such protection was given. I would ask that they let us have that information now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
You had an answer this
afternoon.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I will not keep on repeating the same thing several times. I have said on two occasions in this debate that I have given the house all the information at my disposal at this time. My hon. friend asks for information, but I regret that I am unable to give him more than I have given. I repeat that I have given all that is in my possession and that I will do the best I can to get additional information which is in my department concerning this transaction.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I ask the minister what was
the underlying government policy in giving the protection of the Canadian flag to these ships? What was the reason that was done?
I think that is a very material question. Here was a decision and an unusual exemption granted. What was the policy which caused that to be done? There must have been some reason that the government took that step. Why was it taken? It certainly was not merely to help out a private company, I would think. What was the reason that this unusual step was taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
My hon. friend will have to ask that of some other minister. I did say [Mr. Green.l

this afternoon that the circumstances surrounding the application were that the ships were likely to fall into communist hands; that unless something were done to give the protection of the Canadian flag or the British flag that would happen. I also said that there were no British officers, that is mates or engineers, available in Hong Kong for the manning of these ships.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: What difference would it make to Canada if these Chinese ships did fall into communist hands? These were ships which had never been registered as Canadian ships, except perhaps during the course of their building. They were registered as Chinese ships under the Chinese nationalist government. Why did the government of Canada take this step in order to prevent these ships falling into the hands of the other Chinese government? What was the reason for doing that?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce covered that in his statement last night and if the hon member will look at page 4124 of Hansard he will find the answer.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Is the answer because the dominion government had guaranteed the bank loan? Is that what the Minister of Transport means?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: If my hon. friend is trying to get from me information concerning finance, then I am afraid I cannot give it to him. I have dealt with the matter as far as I can as it concerns the Department of Transport.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
In the course of his remarks a little earlier the Minister of Transport, referring to what the hon. member for Lake Centre had said, -made the statement that the circumstances surrounding this transaction and its present development were not as extraordinary as the hon. member for Lake Centre and those associated with him would lead us to believe. As a matter of fact I think the committee will probably decide that on the contrary the circumstances are more extraordinary than the ministers who have spoken so far this afternoon are prepared to admit. Indeed the circumstances have been extraordinary ever since the inception of this whole transaction which has landed us where we are today.
We have heard about five ships and two ships which appear to have gone missing.
I believe that there were more ships than that. I should like to hear from the government as to what has happened to the other ships which were purchased by this Ming Sung Industrial Company Limited under a government-guaranteed loan. I believe that there were more ships and I should like to

have confirmation of that and to know what has happened to them. Are they in communist hands? Why were they not included in this arrangement? Are they trading with the enemy? What has happened to them?
In a further reference to the questions asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre the Minister of Transport stated that the government did not know anything about the incorporation of the Canadian subsidiary and that he did not know whether it was a dominion or provincial company. Surely the government must have known and must have had information at the time. I am not saying that the minister should remember all the details, but the government surely must have known at the time of the circumstances of this incorporation of the Canadian subsidiary because they had an outstanding loan against these ships.
If the bill of sale of the ships to be registered was in the name of the Canadian subsidiary, surely the government must have had knowledge of that bill of sale at the time they were registered and thus have known of the Canadian subsidiary. If my recollection serves me correctly, it could not have been a provincial company. As I understand the British North America Act, any firm engaged in trans-ocean or inter-coastal shipping could not possibly be incorporated under a provincial charter. It must be a firm incorporated under a dominion charter because the dominion has exclusive jurisdiction over that type of shipping. The federal government must have known at the time when this firm was incorporated. I do not think the committee should be satisfied with the refusal of information at this time on the ground, "Well, we probably do not know anything about it anyway because it may not even have been a dominion charter".

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:

interrupt the hon. member, but I should like to bring to his attention a few citations which I think are appropriate on this occasion. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I recall no occasion on which
it has been said that all the information now available is before us. It has been said-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:

that is exactly what I want to point out. It is one thing for a minister to say that he has given to the house what he knows himself. The minister has a file on the Ming Sung Company. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Perhaps the leader of the opposition did not hear a few words of what I said. I am pretty sure I said that. I think the typescript copy of Hansard will prove I said that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to split hairs, but there is a vast difference between saying that we have all the information that is available at this time and saying that we have all the information that the minister now possesses, or everything he knows at this time. What I am saying is that it is unthinkable that there is not full information in a file in the Department of Transport with respect to the Ming Sung transaction. I qualify that by saying that the minister thinks that it was an oral directive, and if so then it is absolutely certain that there is a file readily available which

Supply-External Affairs will contain the letter or letters which interpreted that oral directive and told the Ming Sung Company the exact conditions under which they would be able to carry out this change of registry.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I think that the leader of the opposition must have been out of the house when, over and above what he repeated, I added that I would get any other information that was available.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Get it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that at the time you referred to certain citations I was dealing with the reasons advanced by the minister in support of the proposition that very probably this information was not in the possession of the government at all, and would not have been in the possession of the government at that time. I said that it might not be at the moment in the personal possession of the minister, but 1 was trying to show that the general information which we are seeking must be in the possession of the government for the reasons I advanced. The minister made other statements this afternoon concerning which I do not think any questions have been asked him yet, and as to which I would think he would have the information available now. I will ask him the questions and then perhaps he can tell us whether he can answer them now or later. One of the questions was actually asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and has not yet been answered or referred to in the minister's reply.
What power has the minister under the Canada Shipping Act to strike these ships off registry? It has been suggested that that should be done, and suggested very strongly for reasons which have, been advanced. The minister has not yet stated what power he has, and what he would have to go through to do that. The other matter to which I should like to refer is that the minister stated very clearly that at the time the exemption was applied for he had doubts as to whether the exemption should be granted, and because of those doubts he referred the matter to his colleagues in the cabinet. That was the minister's statement this afternoon. I can only presume that when he made it he recollected the doubts that he had. I should like to ask him therefore what were the doubts? Why did the minister think that it might not be proper, wise or propitious to grant this exemption? What were the doubts, and what was the basis upon which those doubts came into his mind? I think that is very pertinent indeed because in this case 

the minister appears to have been wiser than his colleagues. If he had doubts one must assume they were removed by his colleagues whereas actually his doubts were correct and the decision of the cabinet seems to me to have been shown to be wrong. I should like to ask the minister at this time to answer these questions. Then there are some further questions that I think should be put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs regarding the transaction. Perhaps the Minister of Transport would be kind enough to answer these questions first.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
With reference to the first
part of the hon. member's statement in which he referred to me as having said that there was nothing extraordinary about the transaction, I think if he looks up Hansard he will find that I was referring to the first part of this application. When I made that statement I was dealing with an application to register a ship under the Canadian flag. I stated that there was nothing extraordinary about that because that is done in the usual manner, and I tried to explain how it was done, by the filing of the bill of sale in the usual office. I am asked what power there is to withdraw. I presume there is the same power as there is to grant an exemption.
In so far as doubts are concerned, I suppose if my hon. friend were to continue his probing he could ask additional questions as to what other things were in my mind at the time. I do not know that I am required to give to the committee what the doubts were that were in my mind, if there were any doubts. What I stated was that usually an application under 133A is dealt with in the discretion of the minister in the ordinary manner, and as a rule I do not submit them to cabinet. In this case I felt that it should be submitted, and I did so. I do not think I need go beyond that. I do not think I am under cross-examination in the committee. I think that when I state that these were the circumstances I have gone as far as any minister is required to go. So far as giving the doubts that might have emerged in my mind at the time, I do not know that I would remember all of them that came up twelve, fifteen or sixteen months ago. Therefore I think I have discharged my responsibility to this house in giving the information which I have.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
The purpose of the question

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN

member for Vancouver-Quadra and, I think, in answer to another hon. member prior to six o'clock. That is a matter of record.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I do not think the minister
has been asked this question. Does the minister know who the directors are of the present affiliated Canadian company?

obtained but I do not know at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:

this time of the directors of the Canadian corporation which made the application in March of 1950. I could hardly be expected to have that recollection.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
There are
one or two questions I should like to ask the Minister of Transport. I should like to know where these ships were when application was made to have them registered in Canada. maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN

registered.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: There is another point I wish to put before the minister. speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is going a bit far when he asks whether I really believed it. Otherwise I would not have submitted the application for the exemption to my colleagues and granted the exemption. maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I was not
casting doubt upon the minister's integrity, but he will remember that he said this was over a year ago and it was difficult for him to remember. Does he not recall that last year we had a very difficult unemployment situation in this country, with 400,000 people [DOT] drawing relief? There must have been thousands of engineers, mates, officers and crew members available at that time to man these seven ships The lakes were closed, navigation on the St. Law'rence was closed, and men must have been available. That is why I would like the minister to produce the correspondence with the Ming Sung Company in regard to this whole matter so the house may judge whether the decision was properly made.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I wanted to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs some questions, but if hon. members have other questions to ask the Minister of Transport perhaps I should wait. The circumstances surrounding this transaction, which have been referred to by the parliamentary assistant, as he has pointed out are recorded in Hansard for April 7, 1949. According to those circumstances it would appear that there is a considerable obligation outstanding against these ships on the part of the government of Chiang Kai-shek. I should like to know the circumstances surrounding that obligation; what negotiations we are conducting with
4194	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs that government and why, if this is the situation-and if it is not I hope the minister will tell the house-and this obligation is guaranteed in part by this government, these ships in which the Canadian government has a very heavy financial interest are permitted, while under the Canadian flag, to trade with people who are at present engaged in hostilities against Canadian troops. Instead of being under the control of the government which made the loan available so the ships might in fact be delivered to the Ming Sung Company, they are now under control of the company and trading with the communist government of China. Ships made available through moneys advanced by the Canadian government on the request of the nationalist government of China, for which that government is liable under the terms of the guarantee, are now trading with what is in effect the enemy. I should like the minister to explain that situation and tell us what negotiations are going on with the Chiang Kai-shek government with respect to that liability.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I do not think I am capable of explaining all the financial details of this transaction, which took place some years ago. No doubt when the Department of Finance estimates are brought forward the hon. gentleman will have an opportunity to get this information.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I might save some time if I
make it clear that I am not asking for the details surrounding the financial transaction.
I am asking what negotiations are in process or 'what contacts we have with the Chiang Kai-shek government regarding the outstanding liability. I am also asking why these ships, on which the Chiang Kai-shek government has a liability to us, are now being allowed to trade with the enemy of that government, a country whose soldiers are fighting Canadian soldiers.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
As far as I know, the Chiang Kai-shek government, which is the government of China we still recognize, has no connection with or liability or obligation in regard to this transaction. As to the statement by the hon. gentleman that we are giving permission for these ships to trade with communist China, which is fighting us in Korea, these ships have no permission that is not granted to any other Canadian ship, and they are not in a special position of any kind. Under Canadian law there is no embargo on shipments to China except in respect of a list of strategic materials; and we have been informed that this list of strategic materials is being recognized by the owners and operators of these ships.
TMr. Fulton.]

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I should like to correct the
minister in both those statements, because they are directly at variance with the facts as disclosed by the record. The minister has just said that as far as he knows the Chiang Kai-shek government has no liability in connection with these ships. When the matter was being discussed in April, 1949, on several occasions the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that the Canadian government stepped in at least in part at the request of the Chiang Kai-shek government, and that the advance made by the banks was guaranteed jointly by the government of Canada and the government of Chiang Kai-shek. So the minister's statement on the first point is not in accord with what we were told two years ago.
Then the minister said these ships were not in a different position and enjoyed no special permission with respect to trading with communist China than any other ship under the Canadian flag. I point out to him that they are in a very special position. They are under the Canadian flag, it is true, but they are manned by Chinese; and the suggestion has been made that one of the captains is a Russian. That has been neither confirmed nor denied.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: It has been denied.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
But they are manned by
Chinese crews, and as far as we know by Chinese communist crews. Apparently they trade freely with communist China, and as far as I know they are the only ships under the Canadian flag carrying on that trade today. So certainly they are in a far different position than any other ship under our flag. I would like the minister, if he will, to reconcile the statements he has made with those earlier statements, and to say what is the present position in that regard.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: If I said the Chiang Kai-shek government had no obligation in regard to this transaction, possibly that was inaccurate. I might have been more accurate in saying that the Chiang Kai-shek government now accepted no obligation in respect of those ships, which have been transferred to Canadian registry. As far as the second question is concerned, these ships are subject to Canadian regulations, and are in exactly the same position legally as any other ship under Canadian registry.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I take considerable objection to the statement by the minister that these ships are in no different position than any other ships flying the Canadian flag. The hon. member for Kamloops has already pointed out one essential difference. Another

difference which is even more essential is that these ships are owned by the Ming Sung Company, whose headquarters as far as I know are in communist China. As a matter of fact I believe they are in Chungking.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: They are in Montreal.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I believe the headquarters of this company are at Chungking. They have a Canadian subsidiary in Montreal. They have another subsidiary at Hong Kong, and so on; but actually the people who own these ships have their headquarters at Chungking as far as I know, and they are completely under the thumb of Mr. Mao. That puts these ships in a totally different position than any other ships flying the Canadian flag. In those circumstances they are really under the control of Mao and his communist Chinese government. Any orders they give in connection with these ships are carried out, I imagine, and will continue to be carried out unless our government steps in and seizes them, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, or brings them back under Canadian control. Apart from that these ships are flying our flag while actually under the command of the rulers of communist China.
There is one other matter on which I should like to comment during this debate. When speaking of the exemptions that he gave to this company, the Minister of Transport made quite a point of the fact that the names put in for these exemptions were Chinese. He seemed to be concerned at that time with disproving the statement made in the letter read by the member for Nanaimo that one of these captains was a Russian. The thing that struck me in connection with that was, why did the fact that the names of the officers of these ships were Chinese give the minister the idea that the exempting of these ships from Canadian law was the right thing to do, in view of the fact that at that time Mao was in control of China? Chiang Kai-shek had been expelled from China, and Mao and the communists were in control. The fact that the names of the captains submitted to the minister were Chinese I would have thought would 'have caused him to question the advisability of waiving the law in favour of these people.
It seems to me that does not in the least explain why this permission was given. It just makes the thing more obscure than ever. I am quite sure that the directive which has been requested exists. I do not understand why, during the three hours from six o'clock until nine o'clock when the committee resumed its business, this directive could not be secured. If it is not a written
Supply-External Affairs directive, at any rate there must have been a note made of it in the proceedings of the cabinet. I cannot understand why, within those three hours, either the written directive, or the stenographic note made of the fact that there was a directive, has not been produced for us to see. Then, we would know what the situation is. It seems to me that until either the directive or the note made of it has been produced, the government is being anything but frank in its disclosures in connection with the whole matter.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
There are one or two questions I should like to ask the Minister of Transport in order to get the matter elucidated. I am not one who does not believe the minister has acted in anything but the best of good faith. Apparently these nine ships were constructed in 1948 and 1949 specifically for this river trade or the trade on the China seas. I understand that any ships trading on the Yangtze have to be specially constructed, and therefore at the commencement of the laying of the keels for these ships the trade they were going to enter must have been fully understood by the government, the banks, the ship contractors, the Chinese company and everyone else connected with them. The use to which these ships were going to be put must have been known for a considerable time.
I understand that there were the seven ships in question, and the two others making up the nine are presently under Panamanian registry and are undertaking this trade. The first question I should like to have answered, therefore, if it is possible, is whether the other ships were built under the same financial guarantee as those ships now plying the Chinese trade to which reference has been made this afternoon. In this connection, I should like to quote an editorial in a periodical known as the Syren and Shipping, which is generally accepted as the spokesman for British shipbuilding. The article is in the May 16 issue. The first two paragraphs describe the restrictions and regulations put on shipments from Hong Kong, and the inspection and care taken to see that contraband is not shipped directly to communist China. I mention these first two paragraphs, because I do not want to distort what this semi-official periodical has to say. This is headed "The Truth About Hong Kong," and in the third paragraph, which is headed "China's Attitude", it says:
China has all .along kept very quiet about Hong Kong, as it has been of such use as a trading post for international trade-not for war stores, because of the effective control we have described-but for domestic purposes.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: -but if I were interested in running a shipping line, I would damn well know what business my ships were in.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: If I were running a shipping business, I would know what cargoes my ships were carrying; and if I were responsible for looking after the granting of indemnities to ships, I would know what was happening.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: It will be a long time before you are running one.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: It is a strange thing, Mr. Chairman, but the Greeks had a word for people who made baa-baa noises in the back row. They called them barbarians. We merely call them heathen Chinese.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Having been the first member to introduce the storms of the south China seas to the calm waters of this committee, Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a few words before you rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Or carry the item.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
When the committee reassembled after the break for the luncheon hour, the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to the fact that he had lost

his usual composure just before the committee rose for lunch. During that brief period in which he was speaking before lunch he suggested that I should feel sorry for the statements I had made. He suggested that I would rue the day. He did not use those words, but in his remarks he most definitely used a tone which was almost threatening, when he said that I should be sorry for the statements which I had made.
I now want to examine the statements which I made-and I was quoting from this letter-just in order to show how far the statements which were made by the general secretary of the navigating and engineer officers guild have been borne out and supported in this discussion. The first point which was brought out in the letter was that vessels of the Ming Sung Industrial Company were trading between Hong Kong, Macao and Canton. Evidence has been produced by ministers here today to show that that statement is correct. The next one was that Canton is a port under the direct control of a government with which the government of the Dominion of Canada has no political relations. I think that statement can be accepted. It has certainly not been denied here today. The third point was: What were these vessels carrying? On the one hand the secretary of the guild reports that eyewitnesses have stated that the daily cargoes included essential war materials. On the other hand we have had produced here today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce a letter from a branch of the company concerned which states that it is not carrying essential war materials out of Hong Kong.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: No, I have not much tjme and I would like to finish what I have to say first. Then you may ask your question.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I thought the hon. member might like to state where the eyewitnesses were located.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
It has been shown that these vessels leaving Hong Kong can go to Macao and then on to Canton. I would like to call attention to the fact that, because of its strategic importance and because of its reputation as a port, although it is not a port of China proper, Macao has been named by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as one of those points to which strategic war materials may not be sent.
So there is at least the -possibility that, having cleared from the Hong Kong government, these ships -could go and pick up essential war materials from Macao for
Supply-External Affairs delivery elsewhere. Because quite obviously it is an entree port into communist China.
The next point was that these vessels are trading under a Canadian flag. This was substantiated here this afternoon time after time.
The fifth is that they are officered and manned by Chinese, and that one has a Russian captain. There is no question about their being officered and manned by Chinese. There has been doubt, in fact it has been emphatically denied, that there is a Russian ca-ptain. Well, it is quite possible that such a mistake could have been made, because it is pretty hard to distinguish between some Russians and Chinese. We must remember that the Mongolian is a Russian, and a Mongolian looks very much like a Chinaman, to those who are not familiar with those people.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Pretty weak!

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Then the next point was that the Ming Sung Company trades in China under the flag of the people's republic of China. There has been evidence today to show that at least two vessels which were taken-if "taken" is the right word-which were operating up the Yangtze, which were built in Canada, and which were included in these original seven or nine vessels which were sold, are still operating on the Yangtze under the flag of the people's republic of China. I do not think that has been denied.
The next point is that the regulations have been evaded. Perhaps "evaded" is not quite the right word, because they were granted exemption from adhering to the Canadian regulations. The average person in Hong Kong would not know that the exemption had been granted. It is quite a reasonable assumption to make that the regulations were being evaded.
There is no question about the concern which such organizations as the merchant navy officers organization, and others, have felt about this matter. So, thus far, I see no cause for great concern on my part. I am not repentant for having brought this matter before the House of Commons. I believe it was my duty to bring it to the attention of hon. members, because it is a serious matter. Because, while there may be some slight inaccuracies, as perhaps have come out

and not yet proved-I still feel that this discussion has brought before the people of Canada a very critical, dangerous, unsatisfactory and, to use the word used last night by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, unhappy situation.
I repeat the request I made earlier in the discussion, that something be done to stop
4198	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs the possibility of this trade going on with Canadian ships in enemy territory. I cannot help accusing the government of being somewhat slack in this matter. They knew that these Canadian ships trading under the Canadian flag were operating in those waters since last summer. They also knew that the Chinese troops started fighting in North Korea last November; and it seems to me rather extraordinary that, so far as we can find out from the discussion today, until a week ago no attempt has been made to try to correct this situation.
I think I have dealt with those points. I do want to stress once again that the ships are operating for this Ming Sung Company- a large company which, as has been admitted today, has ramifications and branches throughout China. I would ask this question: Who is getting the protection from the action of this government? I think it is fairly obvious, in the first place, that the profits accruing from this trade must be going to the directors of the Ming Sung Company. I repeat that it is a company which has branches throughout communist China. Quite obviously if they have their branches in communist China, and if those ships are trading even with the port of Canton, then the communist government of China is also getting the benefit from this trade, because it will be taxing the commodities that come in, and the trade going on. So, from the decision made by this government, it is in some measure enabling the government of a country opposed to our troops in Korea to obtain additional revenue.
Then, thirdly, as to the holders of the mortgage, the various banks which are concerned in this matter, they are getting interest on the principal, the principal being something in the neighbourhood of $12,750,000. They are getting interest on that amount of money.
Those are the three groups which in the main are benefited by the fact that the Canadian government took ships back under the Canadian flag and continued to underwrite the loans which had been made. I was not quite clear on one point when it was stated that the Chiang Kai-shek or nationalist government of China had abrogated its responsibility. I think that is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said with regard to the original guarantee that had been given. Does that mean that Canada has taken over the whole of the guarantee which was given originally?
I understand that Canada accepted only . fifty per cent of that guarantee.
I repeat that far from being penitent, as I think the Secretary of State for External 

Affairs would like me to be, or far from being sorry for having introduced this subject-I do not think he need take that attitude-I think it has been a discussion of value. It has been heated at times, but I do think that it has drawn to the attention of the government and of the people of Canada a situation which needs correcting and which in my humble opinion it is within the power of the government to correct.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
Secretary of State for External Affairs if ships flying the flags of other nations in the United Nations are plying on this triangular route? I refer particularly to ships flying the stars and stripes, or flags of the commonwealth or of France. It seems to me tha. this is a well established trade and that there are ships of many nations, including members of the United Nations, engaged in it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: To the best of my knowledge there are a great many ships still engaged in the China trade. All those members of the United Nations which have accepted the obligation of preventing strategic materials getting to China do not carry such materials on their ships running into communist China at this time. There is no complete embargo on trade with China, so far as I know.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I ask that question to indicate that others are engaged in the same kind of trade.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Reference was made by the
parliamentary assistant to the minister to the debate which took place on April 7, 1949. That debate, of course, did not relate in any way to the major consideration which is before us today.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Oh, yes, it did.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
That debate did not in any
way relate to the transfer of the registry of ships that had been under the control of communist China to Canadian registry, thus being able to fly the Canadian flag.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
You said that the debate
did not in any way relate to this matter. I say it did in some way relate to this matter. Very much did it relate to this matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: If the minister had been listening he would have heard what I said. I said very clearly that it in no way related to the major subject under discussion here, and I made it quite clear what it was and what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: You are remembering it now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
It was the transfer of these ships to Canadian registry. In so far as the interjection made by the parliamentary assistant is concerned, I would point out that he was inaccurate in suggesting that the general debate at that time had disclosed that all these ships had been delivered. It did not. It disclosed the number of ships which were under contract and at that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce expressed the expectation that the contracts would be completed later that year.
We, of course, have not had an opportunity since that time to be informed as to the fulfilment of those details. In so far as the ships which were transferred are concerned, I would suggest that when this item is called again it probably can be disposed of very quickly if the government in the meantime will have obtained the essential information which they have and which they can give to this house. They are in position-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: That is exactly what the Minister of Public Works desired at the beginning of this debate.

maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: You had better run along and get your report.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
The government has simply been evading the real facts in this case and trying to create the pretence that they cannot give information which would fully disclose what is the situation. This is an interesting sequel to the debate in 1949. It was a strange transaction then. This came before the house to ratify an irregular payment by the government. That payment was an obligation that had been incurred in excess of the original contract amount. That was disposed of at that time.
Anyone who wishes to refer to the debate on that day will see that the government was very fully informed in regard to the Ming Sung Company and in regard to the nature of its activities and in regard to where it carried on business. The thing that should be remembered in this is that this is a company primarily operating in communist China. The interesting thing is that the government was prepared to accept a statement from that company delivered to them in Hong Kong as more reliable than a statement sent here by men who were working on these ships or working on ships out of Hong Kong and who, we have every reason to believe, were interested in the welfare of the shipping.
This situation is not merely an incident, it is a symptom of conditions. If this government were really taking a firm stand in regard to communism instead of its attitude in regard to trade with communist China,
Supply-External Affairs this would not have happened, and we would not so easily have made this of definite advantage to a company now operating within communist China.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
